lead: Three transforms on a logo — shift, turn, shrink — cost three matrix-vector products per vertex if applied one at a time. Multiply the matrices once into a single M and each vertex costs one product instead. The factors are written in reverse of the order they act: the matrix nearest the point, on the right, acts first. This chapter gives that rule, shows why swapping two transforms changes the drawing, and builds rotation about a fixed point from three matrices. Only a few universities teach this composition step in detail.
prereq: You need the single transforms from 2.1 and the 3×3 homogeneous form from 2.2.

sections.h3: The rule: multiply in the order you apply

blocks.text: A vertex is a column vector p = (x, y, 1)ᵗ in homogeneous coordinates. If M₁ acts first and M₂ second, p′ = M₂ · (M₁ · p). Multiplication is associative, so M₂ · M₁ · p = (M₂ · M₁) · p: one 3×3 matrix M = M₂ · M₁ does both jobs in a single multiply.

blocks.where: M is the combined matrix; M<sub>1</sub> is applied first and sits rightmost; M<sub>n</sub> is applied last and sits leftmost; n is the number of transforms.

items: Read the product right to left: the rightmost matrix touches the point first.
M is 3×3 in 2D and 4×4 in 3D, as in 2.4.

sections.h3: Order matters: rotation and scaling do not commute

blocks.text: Swapping two factors usually changes the product. Take the 2×2 rotation R = R(90°) and the 2×2 scaling S.

blocks.where: R turns points 90° counter-clockwise; S scales x by 2 and y by 3; the products differ, so the order of application changes the drawing.

blocks.text: Translation behaves the same way in 3×3 form. Shifting then rotating is not rotating then shifting, because a shift that happens first is itself turned by the later rotation.
R(θ) turns points about the origin. To turn about a pivot (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>), carry the pivot to the origin, rotate there, then carry it back.

items: Translate by (−p<sub>x</sub>, −p<sub>y</sub>) so the pivot lands on the origin.
Rotate by θ about the origin.
Translate by (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>) to put the pivot back.

blocks.where: T(a, b) is the 3×3 translation by (a, b); R(θ) is rotation about the origin by θ counter-clockwise; (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>) is the fixed point, which maps to itself.

blocks.text: Put S(s<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>y</sub>) in the middle and the same three matrices scale about a fixed point. Reflection in an arbitrary line follows one recipe: translate the line to the origin, rotate it onto the x-axis, reflect in the x-axis, undo both. Five matrices.

For n vertices and k transforms, applying each transform in turn costs k·n matrix-vector products. Building M first costs k−1 products of 3×3 matrices plus n matrix-vector products. With k = 3 and n = 10,000 that is about 10,000 matrix-vector products instead of 30,000, plus two cheap 3×3 matrix products to build M once. An animation loop rebuilds M only when a transform value changes.

figure.caption: Rotating (3, 1) by 90° about the pivot (1, 1) in three moves: shift to (2, 0), turn to (0, 2), shift back to (1, 3). Multiplied together right to left, T(1,1) · R(90°) · T(−1,−1) is one matrix M that does the same turn, the dotted arc, in one multiply.

spec.aria: A grid with the pivot (1,1) circled and the point (3,1) moving through (2,0) and (0,2) to (1,3) in three numbered arrows, a dotted arc about the pivot from (3,1) to (1,3), and the matrix M = [0 −1 2; 1 0 0; 0 0 1] beside it.

examples.question: Rotate the point (3, 1) by 90° counter-clockwise about the fixed point (1, 1). (a) Do it in three steps. (b) Build the single 3×3 matrix M and check that M · (3, 1, 1) gives the same point.
steps: Translate the pivot to the origin: (3 − 1, 1 − 1) = (2, 0).
Both routes agree, so M is correct.
examples.answer: The rotated point is (1, 3), and M = [[0, −1, 2], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]] reproduces it.
examples.check:
import math
px, py = 1, 1
x, y = 3, 1
t = math.radians(90)
R = [[math.cos(t), -math.sin(t), 0], [math.sin(t), math.cos(t), 0], [0, 0, 1]]
T1 = [[1, 0, px], [0, 1, py], [0, 0, 1]]
T0 = [[1, 0, -px], [0, 1, -py], [0, 0, 1]]
def mul(A, B):
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
M = mul(T1, mul(R, T0))
for row in M:
    print(round(row[0]), round(row[1]), round(row[2]))
v = [x, y, 1]
res = [sum(M[i][k] * v[k] for k in range(3)) for i in range(3)]
print(round(res[0]), round(res[1]), round(res[2]))

traps: Writing M = T · R when the translation happens first. The factor nearest the point, on the right, acts first, so the translation sits on the right: M = R · T.
Shifting the pivot the wrong way: the first matrix is T(−p<sub>x</sub>, −p<sub>y</sub>), not T(p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>).
Mixing conventions. With p as a column vector M sits left of p; with a row vector the whole product reverses.
Feeding degrees to sin and cos in code that expects radians, or dropping the third row (0, 0, 1) so the result is no longer 3×3.

quiz.q: State the composition rule for M₁ applied first and M₂ second.
quiz.a: M = M₂ · M₁. The first-applied factor sits on the right.

quiz.q: Why do R(90°) · T(2, 0) and T(2, 0) · R(90°) send (1, 1) to different points?
quiz.a: First product: shift to (3, 1), then rotate to (−1, 3). Second: rotate to (−1, 1), then shift to (1, 1).

quiz.q: Rotate (2, 0) by 90° counter-clockwise about the fixed point (1, 1).
quiz.a: Shift to (1, −1); rotate to (1, 1); shift back to (2, 2).

quiz.q: Build one matrix that scales by 2 in both directions about the fixed point (2, 3).
A model has 50,000 vertices and three transforms. Compare composing once against applying each transform per vertex.
quiz.a: Per-vertex route: 3 × 50,000 = 150,000 matrix-vector products. Composed route: two 3×3 matrix products plus 50,000 matrix-vector products. The saving grows with k.

quiz.q: How would you build a reflection about the line y = x from basic matrices?
quiz.a: Rotate the line by −45° onto the x-axis, reflect in the x-axis, rotate back by 45°: M = R(45°) · F<sub>x</sub> · R(−45°).

beyond: Not for the exam. Every renderer keeps a matrix stack: a scene graph walks from root to leaf, multiplying each node's local transform into a running matrix, so a chair inside a room inside a building costs one matrix per vertex. The GPU receives a single 4×4 model-view-projection matrix as a shader input, which is why this rule is the first thing a shader programmer uses. Animation systems blend per-bone matrices.
